content.content:
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution. When the owner asks for a change, don't begin implementing it until the two of you share an explicit understanding of the problem it's meant to solve **and** have agreed that the requested change is the best way to solve it — a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Treat the request as a description of a desired outcome, not a specification to execute on sight; surface your read of the problem, raise a better approach if you see one, and reach consensus first. This applies to any repository, not just this one.

An interactive comment from the owner carries one of three build-relevant intents — or none of them — and the classification decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part) — the assessment itself stays judgment.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched — the artifact changes as much as the correction demands; what doesn't appear is a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — a feature run: agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Once the intent is understood, author the assurance first: the check the future world must satisfy. Execute it and watch it fail — the failure is the evidence it detects exactly what the owner was worried about — and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the same step is demonstrating the gap: show the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it. A fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for — and an unrouted comment tends to become a one-off patch where a requirement or a rule should have accumulated.

Confirm a behavior isn't already provided before building a mechanism for it — verify the gap against a real run first; the cheapest fix is often that it already works.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, don't reflexively expand the artifact to compensate. First check whether it's already correct — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong (the sibling of the rule above). And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs — prose padded to preempt confusion usually breeds it.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Build from the source, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong; a clean-room rebuild catches biases an edit-in-place pass silently inherits.

Fix build/test/CI warnings, don't tolerate them: a clean run with no warnings makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out, so noise here costs detection later. Prefer a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix: it hides the signal instead of resolving it. Never reach for suppression as the quick path — it's only ever a deliberate, reviewed decision, made once the real fix has been weighed and rejected, never an unattended default. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: an explanation on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected. That inline reason *is* the review record — it's what separates a considered suppression from a reflexive mute, and it's why the suppression needs no second justification recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current. It reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it (unless one is already open) so it's tracked and not lost — then move on. Resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; don't carry one approval forward, and don't treat a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt as authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action. When in doubt, surface the new state and wait for a fresh approval.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project; this section keeps the method. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

{"number":577,"title":"Claudinite growth: promote 5 lessons to canon (d2026-07-30)","body":"Refs #574

Promote run over the 11 Context members' local packs. Five lessons admitted; all landed at the **prose** rung (each is in-flight agent behaviour or runtime state with no repo-state signature, so no check could carry it).

| Origin | Lands in | Generalized rule |
|---|---|---|
| TLDR | `packs/basics/RULES.md` (fold) | The `Comment class:` declaration goes alone on its line — the line is scanned for every class token, so restating the menu to rule options out declares them all, and the append-only transcript makes it unfixable later. |
| TLDR | `unattended-agents` | Dispatch a subagent that may commit under worktree isolation, or the parent's checkout is left on the child's branch and branch-scoped end-of-session checks judge the child's commits against the parent's transcript. |
| GoogleCalendarEventCreator | `unattended-agents` | A routine that correctly declines has not failed: record the reason on the item, mark it for a human, exit zero. Failing raises a second triage signal and reports the pipeline as broken. |
| gRatio | `unattended-agents` | When the outcome the ceiling names is mechanically unavailable, stop short and say so — never substitute a riskier action (self-merging an unreviewed PR) to close the gap. |
| gRatio | `writing-tests` | Run a slow suite as its own command with an explicit timeout above its measured runtime, install deps in a separate earlier call, and wait on a backgrounded run rather than relaunching. |

Diff is 5 lines across 3 files, all under `packs/`.

**Notable rejections** (all duplicates found by the whole-corpus dedupe, not portability failures) — capping/qualifying GitHub MCP list+search calls and `git checkout <ref> -- <paths>` destroying uncommitted edits are both already in `git-github-advanced`; `git ls-files` not covering brand-new untracked files is in `engineering-practices`; the prose deletion test is in `prose-to-checks`; "a pack carries how we work, never what the product does" is in `generate-project-instructions`; the high-watermark re-anchoring caveat is in `writing-tests`. No stub pack was minted.

{"number":684,"title":"basics: minimize task shelf-life — watch changes work now, never "check tomorrow"","body":"Comment class: process-change.

Owner rule (2026-08-07): every task's shelf-life — from starting it until everyone can forget it — is minimized. "Check tomorrow" is almost always the wrong choice in any context: it costs a full reload of context that was free while the work was hot. So a change to scheduled/unattended machinery is verified by **forcing a run now** (`FORCE_TASKS`, `workflow_dispatch`, the fleet force sweep) and watching it to a terminal state; migration plans prefer one forced convergence pass over nightly trickle, accept legacy at the door, and drive stragglers with a mechanism, not a remembered phase. When "now" is impossible, the follow-up must be a mechanism that comes to you — never a human's memory.

Prose rung of the promotion ladder, deliberately: whether verification was deferred is an in-flight judgment no check can see.

Refs #676.

{"number":751,"title":"growth-promote: dedupe PR #740's rule additions and cut the language","body":"Reviewed rebuild of #740. Every rule addition there was checked for necessity against **current** `main`, the duplicates dropped, and the surviving prose rewritten terse.

Two things forced a rebuild rather than a patch on top of #740's branch:

1. **Its own dedupe was incomplete.** Merging seven branches and keeping "the longest phrasing" left several lessons standing two and three times, and one merge artifact was syntactically broken.
2. **Its base is 40 commits behind `main`.** #740's diff targets a `packs/basics/RULES.md` that still had the engineering-practices bullets in a separate skill file, and an `adopt-pack` whose catalog premise `main` has since invalidated.

## Dropped as duplicate (6)

| Lesson | What #740 did |
|---|---|
| "Not statically checkable" expires | added **3×** to `prose-to-checks` |
| Product-statement counterfactual | added **2×** to `prose-to-checks`, back to back |
| Serialized round-trip comparison | added **2×** to `writing-tests` |
| A skip still exits 0 / self-updating mechanism | added **2× each** to `unattended-agents` |
| Human-only step gets its own issue | added to **both** `basics/RULES.md` and `git-github-advanced` |
| Sibling-repo copy is a canon candidate | added to **both** `basics/RULES.md` and `extracting-lessons.md` |

Also dropped: `unattended-agents`' cap-and-qualify bullet (already canon in `git-github-advanced`, "Cap *and* qualify every list/search call"), and its restatements of the tool-search and summarizing-fetch contracts that now sit once in `basics/RULES.md`.

`prose-to-checks`' severity list was left broken by the merge — item 3 read `directional by kind, or when …` followed by a stray `directional by kind.` from the other side. Repaired.

## Dropped as obsolete (1)

`adopt-pack`'s "the mount holds only what it already adopted, so shallow-clone the canon to enumerate the catalog" is **false on current main**: `compute-vendor-set` ships `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` with every mount, declared packs or none (asserted by `compute-vendor-set.test.mjs:148`). Only the match-the-owner's-plain-words-to-a-pack-id half survives, as one sentence on the existing catalog paragraph.

## Re-homed (2)

#661 folded `skills/engineering-practices/SKILL.md` into `packs/basics/RULES.md`. #740 still edits the deleted file — the landmine its own description flagged. The unknown-state rule and the widened self-description bullet land in `RULES.md` instead.

## Kept, terser

`basics/RULES.md` (dispatch-prompt classification, shared-pack-before-hand-authoring, three harness-tool contracts, text-finding waivers, blocked-host policy boundary, human-only-step issue, unknown-state, multi-site disclosure claims) · `authoring-agent-docs` (withdrawn practices rewritten present-tense) · `writing-tests` (serialized round-trip) · `git-github-advanced` (auto-merge refusals, `.gitignore` pruning trap, green-run-≠-job-ran) · `extracting-lessons` (two kinds that never become a pack rule) · `prose-to-checks` (counterfactual, "already covered" is a claim to test, expiring un-checkability, irreversible-condition severity, positive allowlist, form-not-intent) · `unattended-agents` (skip-in-a-green-run, fresh-context judgment stages, re-issuing rejected guard calls, unedittable tracker posts) · `node` (`node --test` skips dot-directories) · `research-project` (per-input calibration, figure-only methods, explicit gap lists).

## Verification

- `node --test` over `packs-tests/`, `engine-tests/`, `vendoring/`, `dev/` — **1347 pass, 0 fail**.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` — **0 blocking, 17 advisory**; verified identical on a stashed tree, so this change adds none.

{"number":760,"title":"Rewrite RULES.md as situation-keyed rules, and write down the method","body":"`packs/basics/RULES.md` was prose paragraphs and one-rule-per-bullet lists. A reader holding a problem had to find their rule by reading, and a paragraph often carried four or five rules at once.

It is now **61 rules, each opening with the act that triggers it** — so a rule announces itself while you work rather than waiting to be looked up.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Rules | 29 bullets + 20 prose units | 61 |
| Words | 4435 | 2985 (−33%) |
| Longest paragraph | 287 words | — |

## The shape

```
**<the act you are performing[, in the situation that matters]>** — <what to do>;
  <the fallback if you can't>; <the thing the other rules make unnecessary>.
```

A rule keyed to a *state* never fires, because nothing brings the reader to it. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown" — they notice they are writing an encoder. So every subject names an act: `Encoding a value that may be unknown`, `Seeing a build, test or CI warning`, `Wanting to change a class you already declared`, `Handing over a step only a human can perform`.

Within a rule the clauses run best-first: the default, then `if you can't`, then `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary. Modality is graded per clause and never exceeds what the source claimed — `never` survives only where the original said `never`; `prefer`, `avoid`, `rather than`, `don't` and `only when` are each kept where the original used them.

## Commits

1. **Engineering practices → situation blocks** — 29 bullets to 23, 2721 → 1274 words. Four bullets describing one decision (single source of truth, its drift guard, the shared-constants mechanism, "don't also comment it") became one block.
2. **The method, written down** — a `## Shape a rule so it fires` section in the `authoring-agent-docs` skill, which already owns "Write each rule". Marked as house practice, since the rest of that file cites published guidance and this has none. It reconciles with the existing "state the motivation behind a rule": drop rationale that only restates the rule, keep a consequence the reader needs under pressure.
3. **`rules-line-length`** — advisory, 100 bytes, groundwork rather than a reformatting campaign. Authored first and watched fail on 18 files before anything was wrapped. Byte length, not characters: an em dash costs three bytes. Six packs already held to 100, two of them exactly, so this is the corpus's own limit written down. `basics/RULES.md` is wrapped here; the other 17 files are tracked in #766.
4. **Working discipline + task lifecycle → situation rules** — 20 prose units to 38 rules. The classification paragraph alone held four rules; the shelf-life paragraph held five.
5. **Trim** — rationale that only explains is gone from 15 rules.
6. **Subjects** — 20 that named a state now name the act.

Blank lines separate rules throughout, for reading.

## What is preserved

Every rule. Every operative literal the checks pointing at this file depend on: the exact `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` line, the alone-on-the-line scanning rule, the three classes' obligations, `FORCE_TASKS`, and the `Refs #123` / `Fixes #123` / `Closes #123` forms.

Exceptions that change what a reader does are kept as part of their rule — a correction never adds a new requirement; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place; the exception for a human step whose home is an artifact the human is already editing.

## What left the prose

Rationale that only explains ("an open task is a standing tax…", "the transcript is append-only", "reading the draft first anchors you to its framing"), worked examples, and check parameters recoverable from the check itself — `.claudinite-checks.json` as a path, the `value`/`counts`/`what` fields and `regex: true` now live with the `sharedConstants` check, whose own source comment documents them.

Kept, because each changes what a reader does rather than reassuring them: "copying a mechanic from a sibling repo is the tell that it belongs centrally"; "the bare short name returns 'no matching tools', which reads exactly like absence"; "a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first"; "a waiver is for a crossing that genuinely must exist".

## Structural changes worth a look

- **The comment classes lost their numbering.** They were a numbered list and the process-change rule said "take it to mode 2"; they are now `Acting on a correction / a feature / a process change`, and the reference reads "take it to the feature path". Nothing outside this file referenced the numbering.
- **`Three harness-tool contracts` became a `## Harness-tool contracts` heading.** With a blank line between every rule, three consecutive bullets no longer read as one run.
- **The lifecycle's numbered steps stayed tight** — one ordered procedure, not three rules.

## Verification

- 1417 tests pass; `check_the_world` reports 0 blocking
- the catalog tally in `packs/README.md` moved 82 → 83 for the new check, caught by its own drift guard rather than by hand
- an automated audit confirms all 61 subjects are action-anchored, and that 26 operative literals survive
- the rewrap asserts the whitespace-normalised prose is unchanged before and after, which caught a tokenizer bug that duplicated adjacent code spans (`` `cat`/`grep`/`sed` ``)

The 34 advisories are 17 pre-existing and 17 from the new rule, all in files #766 covers.

{"number":857,"title":"Where CI time goes: fixture signing, the fleet-wide numbers, and a weekly measurement","body":"Fixes #855. The breakdown you asked for, the one real find in it, and the standing mechanism so the next answer doesn't come from a hand-run investigation.

## The breakdown

CI job ~60s: checkout 3–5s, setup-node 5s, **unit tests 48s**, conformance sweep 1–2s, the two gates ~0s. Only the test step is worth profiling.

Under CI-like conditions the suite is **146s serial across 142 files**, and the distribution is the interesting part: not a few slow tests, but **583 tests in the 200ms–1s band** — the signature of a fixed per-test cost in a shared fixture helper, which is where the find was.

## Fleet-wide: already fast, and now recorded

Measured first, since it was named the priority. What every member actually runs:

| surface | cost |
|---|---|
| `check_the_work` (Stop hook, every session) | 235ms |
| `check_the_world` (converge / CI) | ~800ms, of which **88ms is rule execution** |
| `discoverPacks` / `buildContext` | 58ms / 41ms |

37 rules, slowest `pack-discovery-entry-await` at 63ms. The rest of the ~800ms is Node startup plus the eager pack-tree import. There is nothing to win here, and members carry smaller pack sets than the canon, so they pay less. Recording the numbers is the deliverable — it stops this being re-profiled.

## The find: fixture commits were being signed

`makeRepo` pins identity and auto-gc but inherited the host's `commit.gpgsign`, so in a session with signing configured every fixture commit became a round trip to a signing service — **202ms per fixture against 38ms without**, and the local suite **71s → 52s**.

Runners have no signing configured, so **CI never paid this**. That is also the explanation for the gap in the last PR, where local showed 33% and CI 10%: the local box was dominated by a cost CI does not have. Both numbers are stated separately throughout rather than letting the flattering one stand.

It is still worth fixing — every agent session in this repo pays it, and the degraded-service failure mode is worse than slow: each commit blocks and leaks descriptors until git fails process-wide, for reasons pointing nowhere near the code under test. The test pins the **isolation**, not the speed — it forces a hostile ambient config (signing on, program `/bin/false`) and requires the fixture to build anyway, so it means the same thing on a runner. Seen failing first (`gpg failed to sign the data`).

## What this PR does *not* do any more

An earlier commit promoted that lesson into `basics/writing-tests` as a portable practice. Reviewed and reverted in the same PR: **every** caller of `makeRepo` is a Claudinite conformance-check test, there are none in `packs/` or `engine/` product code, and a member's app tests have no reason to build a git repo — the fixture is a repo only because the subject under test takes a repo as input, which is this project's business alone. The local pack's "portable candidate" marker was itself the misjudgment, inherited rather than tested.

It needs no prose home at all now: the helper pins the config and `engine-tests/helpers-git-fixtures.test.mjs` goes red if that is removed. A guarded invariant belongs on the strongest rung of the ladder, not restated as prose that every session pays for.

## A negative result, reported rather than shipped

=== skills/fetching-from-the-web/SKILL.md
---
name: fetching-from-the-web
description: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
metadata:
  body: guidelines
  usage:
    expect: triggered
  force-load-on-tool-calls:
    - 'WebFetch'
    - 'Bash.command /(^|[;&|]\s*|\n\s*)(curl|wget)\b/'
  force-load-on-tool-results-matching:
    - 'WebFetch /EGRESS_BLOCKED|\b403\b/'
    - 'Bash /EGRESS_BLOCKED|HTTP\/[\d.]+ 403\b|\b403 Forbidden\b|status(?: code)?:? 403\b/'
---

# Fetching from the web

- **Needing exact text** — a summarizing fetch tool is not a source; when the bytes matter, `curl`
  into the scratchpad and read from disk. (needing-exact-text)
- **A `403`** — don't retry and don't try a sibling URL; attribute the search snippet to the
  publisher instead of asserting it, and mark it for re-verification. (a-rule)
- **A sandbox or proxy denial is a policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around** — no
  open-network runner, no ad-hoc CI workflow, no push-triggered probe to make the request from
  somewhere the policy does not apply. Answer from committed reference material or ask the owner,
  and say plainly that anything unverifiable is unverified. (sandbox-proxy-denial)
- **An explicit egress block** (`EGRESS_BLOCKED`) is domain-wide, unlike a publisher's `403`:
  working down alternate sources for the same fact spends the same denial on each. Never file the
  gap as "re-verify next pass" — no later agent pass can cross a policy block either; mark it as
  needing a human or an unblocked environment. (explicit-egress-block)
=== skills/searching-for-a-tool/SKILL.md
---
name: searching-for-a-tool
description: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
metadata:
  body: guidelines
  usage:
    expect: triggered
  force-load-on-tool-calls:
    - 'ToolSearch'
  force-load-on-tool-results-matching:
    - 'ToolSearch /no (matching )?tools/i'
---

# Searching for a tool

- **A search that finds nothing** is evidence about your query, not about the environment: vary
  the query before concluding a capability is absent, and try the tool before telling the owner a
  step is theirs. (search-finds-nothing)
- **`select:` takes a short name as readily as a qualified one** — `select:get_teams` and
  `select:mcp__github__get_teams` both return the tool, and a comma-separated list loads several at
  once. Qualify a name two servers could both carry. (select-takes-short)
- **A bare short name is a keyword query, and resolves too** — `get_teams` on its own returns the
  tool, ranked above the looser matches beneath it. (bare-short-name)
- **A server whose whole roster the deferred-tools listing already names** is the one exception: one
  miss there is the answer, so read the roster rather than rephrase the query. (server-whole-roster)
=== skills/committing/SKILL.md
---
name: committing
description: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
metadata:
  body: guidelines
  usage:
    expect: triggered
  force-load-on-tool-calls:
    - 'Bash.command /(^|[;&|]\s*|\n\s*)git\s+commit\b/'
---

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking. (concern-commit)
- **Reference the issue, when the change has one** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where
  the commit finishes it. A change tracked by its PR alone references nothing.
  (reference-issue-change)
- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
  (landed-commit-revised)
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever
  else was in progress. (stage-name)
=== skills/writing-repo-scanning-checks/SKILL.md
---
name: writing-repo-scanning-checks
description: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
metadata:
  body: guidelines
  usage:
    expect: triggered
  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
    - "**/engine/checks/**"
    - "**/packs/*/worldRules/**"
    - "**/packs/*/workRules/**"
    - "**/packs/*/skills/*/checks.mjs"
    - "**/declared-checks.json"
---

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it. (choosing-file-set)

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either. (scanning-forbidden-token)

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you. (proving-check-silent)
=== skills/working-with-generated-files/SKILL.md
---
name: working-with-generated-files
description: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
metadata:
  body: guidelines
  usage:
    expect: triggered
  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
    - "**/*GENERATED*"
---

# Working with generated files

- **Working with a file a test or tool generates** — put `GENERATED` in its name, and don't
  hand-edit it; change the generator. Never resolve its merge conflict by hand: clear the
  markers with either side, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit that
  output. Consider automating the clear with a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry, and
  `git rerere` for a conflict that recurs. (working-file-test)

- **A generator whose OWN set of outputs grows on its own** — one baseline per auto-discovered
  category (a new test "kind", a new fixture), rather than a fixed, named list — needs its
  `merge=ours` coverage to auto-track that growth too, typically a glob or pattern in
  `.gitattributes` rather than one entry per file. A per-file allowlist silently stops covering
  the moment a new category starts committing its own baselines, and the gap surfaces as a
  binary merge conflict git cannot 3-way-merge at all — at the worst possible moment, mid-merge,
  for a category nobody remembered to wire up. (generator-whose-own)

## PR #941 · 2026-08-18 · Task-owned trackers, and no fallback for a missing required input
- by @missingbulb · model Claude · pack version 5
- the commit trailer references Refs #940 - READ THE PULL REQUEST BODY for the keyword it used and write that into Landed. the two disagree on most older pull requests, the body's Closes being what fills GitHub's Development panel and the trailer's Refs linking nothing there
- ci-performance (reworded)

> * A task's standing tracker is the task's own, resolved in its own prework
>
> Two tasks each carried a private copy of the same tracker search, already
> diverged: one filtered `is:open`, which never matches a tracker at rest and so
> opens a second one the moment anybody closes the first. Both also reported the
> number they resolved as `delivered: { issue }` — a key neither dispatch path
> rendered, so it reached no agent and the agentic phase hunted for the issue by
> title anyway.
>
> The lookup and the create-then-close pair become a library a task's prework may
> call; `delivered.issue` becomes an `Issue:` line in the hand-off, on both paths.
> Nothing in the machinery knows a task keeps a tracker: whether to keep one, and
> whether a run with nothing to say should mint one, stay the task's own calls.
>
> * An agentic phase's required inputs are stated, and a missing one fails the run
>
> An agentic phase has no `throw`, so a worker doc that reads a parameter out of
> its dispatch is the only thing that can supply the stop. Left unsaid, a missing
> input is an invitation to improvise — search the tracker by title, take the
> newest branch, enumerate the fleet — and each of those substitutes another run's
> inputs for this one's while the run still reports success.
>
> Every doc that reads such a parameter now names it required and says what an
> absent one means: converge to needs-human, naming the missing input. Both
> executor briefs carry the general form, so a task that adds a parameter later
> inherits it.
>
> task-phase-discipline read those stops as discretionary skips. It now exempts a
> stop that converges to needs-human — a failure is not a skip — and still flags a
> real skip in a doc that mentions the failure state elsewhere.
>
> ---------

- by @missingbulb · model Claude · pack version 12

- spotting-change-should (born)

> * /do-later: defer a change into a chained, blocked request run
>
> A follow-up spotted mid-session had nowhere to go: implement it now and the
> session derails, file an ordinary issue and it waits for somebody to remember it.
> The request mode (#1010) already turns a marked issue into a queue run — what it
> lacked was a way to say NOT YET, and a way to say YOU NEED NOT ASK ME ABOUT THIS
> ONE. Both ride the vocabulary that already exists.
>
> Not yet is `Blocked-by:`. A marked issue may name what it waits on in the same
> field a work item uses; adoption carries the still-open ones onto the item it
> births, which is born `task:blocked`, and the tick's job 2 releases it when they
> close. So the chain the owner asked for is not a feature: each deferral names the
> previous deferral's issue and the queue serializes them. A blocker already closed
> is dropped rather than born and immediately readied; an unreadable one delays.
>
> "Don't ask me" is `claude-automerge`, consumed with the mark like the model labels
> so no authorization lingers into a later ask, and copied onto the item as
> `Merge: if-narrow`. The built-in task's ceiling becomes `merged-pr` — a maximum,
> not an instruction: with no `Merge:` field the worker opens a pull request and
> parks exactly as before, which is what every ordinary marked issue keeps getting.
>
> Narrow is measured, not judged. narrow-diff.mjs classifies the run's own diff:
> docs, test files and comment-only edits never count, and what remains must be code
> within a single directory. Comment stripping is C-family and reuses the checks
> helper, so a language it does not model counts as code — the safe end of a verdict
> that decides whether a change lands unattended.
>
> The session-side half is the `do-later` skill in claudinite-growth: which blocker
> to name, the model family read off the running session, and the one case that
> withholds the authorization outright — the owner saying they want to review this
> one outranks how small the change looks.
>
> * work-item body tests: the parse result carries the new Merge field
>
> * do-later belongs to basics, and §16.11 states the design rather than its history
>
> Deferring a change is working discipline — the lifecycle move that files work
> instead of doing it now — not authoring Claudinite content, so the skill sits in
> basics beside the rest of the issue/branch/PR lifecycle, with one bullet in that
> section pointing at it.
>
> §16.11 is rewritten as design: what the two new dimensions are, why each rides
> existing vocabulary, why the ceiling has to be a maximum rather than a second
> task, and why the narrow verdict is code rather than the worker's judgment. The
> owner quote and the running commentary are gone, and §16.2 states today's ceiling
> instead of narrating the change to it.
>
> ---------

- by @missingbulb · model Claude Opus 5 · pack version 13

- verifying-now-genuinely (reworded)

> * basics: a change proven only in production files its own verification
>
> The loop that proves a change works stopped at the merge: anything whose
> effect appears elsewhere — a pack reaching a member, a deploy, a rule the
> next session loads — got verified when someone thought to ask.
>
> The skill runs at the end of every change, beside the conversation capture,
> and mostly files nothing: a change watched working, or pinned by a test that
> ran, is already proven. Where it isn't, it files an issue naming the artifact
> that says the change is live and the assertion that proves it works there.
> The task reads that queue daily, stays silent while nothing is live, and
> either proves the change or files what it found instead.
>
> * verify-in-production rides the request lane, not a task of its own
>
> The queue is already the delayed-execution mechanism for ad-hoc work: a
> marked issue is adopted, waits on Blocked-by, and a consumed mark means
> re-marking re-adopts — the whole retry loop in existing vocabulary. The
> standing daily task was a second queue beside it, keyed on a title prefix.
>
> Dropped. The skill now files a deferred request (claude-task, Blocked-by
> the PR, Not-before just past the expected release) whose brief tells the
> run to verify when live, re-arm by bumping its own Not-before and re-mark
> when not, and give up at a stated date. One generic gap closed in the
> engine: adoption now carries a still-future Not-before: from the marked
> issue onto the item, symmetric with Blocked-by — without it a re-marked
> verification is picked within the hour, forever.
>
> * merge-to-main: a recipe, not an explanation
>
> * verify-in-production: automatic end to end, and the run decides nothing
>
> Owner review: the verification is an unattended check by construction —
> Verify: must be a read a run can make, a person only where no automatic
> check can exist. A failure reopens the change's own issue (Original-issue:)
> rather than filing a new one. The give-up marker is dropped, and the re-arm
> extension is the filer's Retry-every: — the run just executes its playbook.
>
> ---------

> Two gaps this session hit while running #1119. The stack of PRs stopped at the
> first gate, so the cleanup and the destructive tail were written later, by
> whoever remembered, at the cost of a second approval. And the execution steps
> were a checklist — "run them at will, in one sitting" is true only when nothing
> has to become observable in between, which in a fleet migration is never.
>
> So the shape is stated once, at the top, and then carried: setup, one approval of
> everything, then a chain that runs itself. All the code is written before the
> owner is asked for anything, the tail included — write is not merge, and what
> waits is the merge. Every step after the approval is filed at plan time as a
> queued continuation on the ad-hoc lane, each naming the previous in `Blocked-by:`

> when its own check passed, because closing is what releases the next. Three
> hazards get named for the same reason — nothing distinguishes a `completed` close
> from a `not planned` one, a link that cannot make its reads must park rather than
> answer "all clear", and every link reports to the tracking issue so the plan and
> the queue never have to be reconciled by hand.

# basics pack

The baseline pack — the `RULES.md` prose every session loads (injected by the pack-prose hook) plus the working-discipline checks. Its subject is **how work is done**, whatever tool is running it. Declared explicitly like every other pack — no pack is active by default; bootstrap seeds the declaration and the nightly baselining backfills it into existing consumers.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Starting any requested change | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| Replying to an owner comment | high | complexity | prose: <200 words |
| Acting on a correction | high | correctness | prose: <50 words |
| Acting on a feature | high | correctness | prose: <50 words |
| Acting on a process change | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| Choosing what goes on that ladder | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| Landing a rule anywhere on the ladder | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| Building a mechanism for a behavior | medium | complexity | prose: <20 words |
| Building release, deploy, versioning or CI plumbing | medium | complexity | prose: <50 words |
| Finishing a change | high | correctness | prose: <50 words |
| Changing scheduled or unattended machinery | high | correctness | prose: <50 words |
| Planning a migration | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words + skill (`writing-migration-plans`) |
| Filing a plan's issues | high | correctness | prose: <100 words + skill (`writing-migration-plans`) |
| Adding a legacy tolerance | high | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| Choosing an automerge policy | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| Predicting an irreversible change | critical | correctness | prose: <50 words |
| Handing over a wider diff than asked | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| Retiring a system into another | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| When verifying now is genuinely impossible | high | correctness | prose: <200 words + skill (`verify-in-production`) |
| Finishing a larger element | medium | correctness | prose: <100 words + skill (`production-retrospective`) |
| Receiving feedback that flags a misunderstanding | medium | complexity | prose: <50 words |
| Writing anything | low | complexity | prose: <20 words |

5235b9d31a184356a9a7c6c34cc11c76fba5a097 2026-06-20 Add portable Claude rules docs

 README.md               |  26 ++++++++++
 agent-architecture.md   |   8 ++++
 agenticBestPractices.md |  28 +++++++++++
 engineeringPractices.md |  30 ++++++++++++
 git-and-github.md       | 124 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 ownerPreferences.md     |  24 ++++++++++
 working-discipline.md   |  26 ++++++++++
 7 files changed, 266 insertions(+)
---
19:- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
20:- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (A UI-snapshot coverage gate parked behavioral leaves `9.1`–`9.3`/`3.4` and an unreachable `8.6` on cases that render none of them — issue #429.)
21:- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
22:- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production.
23:- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
24:- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
26:- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
27:- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.

}

    if m:
        sec = m.group(1) or m.group(2)
    if line.startswith('```entry '):
        el = line[len('```entry '):].strip()
        j = i + 1
        while j < len(lines) and not lines[j].startswith('```'):
            j += 1
        body = lines[i + 1:j]

            i = j + 1
            continue
        nk = KIND.get((sec, el))
        if nk and body and body[0].startswith('## '):
            parts = body[0].split(' · ')
            parts[1] = nk
            body[0] = ' · '.join(parts)

        out.append('```')

    if line.startswith('- **Landed:** ') and sec in LANDED:

            tail = ' · pack version' + rest.split(' · pack version', 1)[1]
        tail = tail.rstrip('.')
        out.append('- **Landed:** ' + LANDED[sec] + tail + '.')
        i += 1
        continue
    out.append(line)
    i += 1

open(OUT, 'w').write('\n'.join(out))
print('wrote', OUT, len(out), 'lines')

## 2026-09-15 · born · converted from references.md (writing-tests-4)
- **Reason:** An audit of the canon's ~3,600 tests found ~30 assertions reading back a value the
  test's own setup had chosen: a declared check's `severity` (a pass-through of the declaration) and
  its `rule` id (the very id the test selected the check by).
- **Mechanism:** prose, a guideline of the writing-tests skill
- **Retire when:** Retire the rule if findings stop carrying fields the engine copies through
  unchanged.
===
## 2026-09-02 · born · converted from references.md (RULES-1)
- **Reason:** Owner decision, set while planning the dashboard chain (#1613): "The owner reviews are
  here not to make sure all code was created perfectly … Your ability to write code at fantastic
  speeds means that making sure a code is perfect is a goal that pales in comparison to get the code
  out the door and working. The things I now care about are much more specific: I fear destructive
  code that deletes data in production, or creates such a bad experience that users leave. Anything
  which isn't easily reversible with another PR. The second thing I care about is growth —
  separation of concerns, making sure the system is simple. Seeing which folders changed tells me a
  lot about if the change made sense; a 3-file change for a change I expected to be a one-liner
  gives me indications not of destructive errors, but of opportunities to learn. So when we create a
  long chain of tasks and set automerge rules — the goal is to have a good prediction of the
  change that would come from a feature request, and if that prediction holds — merge and move on.
  Automerge policy failing is a major speed bump, but it allows us to make sure the wagon is on the
  right trail." Reaffirm while a person still reviews chain PRs by their footprint; retire only if
  the owner redefines what review is for.
- **Mechanism:** prose

  ``[`old/path.md`](../old/path.md)`` holds it in both the visible label and the target — so a
  `sed` anchored on the `](../href)` form rewrites the target and leaves the label reading the old

  backticked label forms need the same rewrite.

  imports and index entries behind that **no test necessarily fails on** — a README docs-index

content.content:
`barrier` is the one check a project has to configure before it does anything: it enforces a
**directed folder-access graph** the repo declares on this pack's entry as `config.barriers.rules`,
and a repo that declares none is silent rather than failing. [barriers.md](barriers.md) is the whole
vocabulary — the rule forms, how a reference is resolved against the tree, the exception kinds, and
how another pack ships a fixed barrier of its own as manifest data. It arrived here when the
`barriers` pack was absorbed (#1681): no project ever chose that pack, it rode in on the baseline's
`requires` closure, and a separate identity for a mechanism everyone already has bought only a
second catalog row and an adoption question nobody had asked for.

`improve-comments-scope` is owned by the
[improve-comments](skills/improve-comments/checks.mjs) skill rather than by this pack's rule
directories, because it validates that skill's action rather than a property of the repo: on a
branch whose commit subject is `Claudinite tidy: improve comments` it strips the comments from both
sides of every changed file and reds anything left over, plus any change at all under
`.claudinite/` — the mount is not the repo's own source. Silent everywhere else, so an ordinary
branch pays nothing for it. The [improve-comments](tasks/improve-comments/README.md) task is what
writes under it, weekly, over the files the window's commits touched. Both arrived here when the
`tidy-repo` pack was retired (#1839): its issue and PR sweeps had been outgrown, and the comment
pass was the one dimension left — baseline housekeeping, with no second declaration to earn.

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking. (concern-commit)
- **Reference the issue, when the change has one** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where
  the commit finishes it. A change tracked by its PR alone references nothing.
  (reference-issue-change)
- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
  (landed-commit-revised)
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever
  else was in progress. (stage-name)

## 2026-07-06 · born · Context-relief architecture: packs (prose + checks) and skills, with enforcement (#128)
- **Reason:** the corpus was reorganized into two homes selected by WHEN a rule is active, and this
  pack is the one that is active in every session: cross-project working discipline, the task
  lifecycle, and the baseline engineering practice, whatever technology is running.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Mechanism:** a pack named `universal`, carrying `RULES.md` prose injected at session start and
  the checks that back it, discovered by a directory scan so there is no list to maintain.
- **Landed:** #128, closing #127 and #131.

## 2026-07-11 · scope-changed · No pack is active by default - the basics pack (né universal) is declared explicitly (#232)
- **Reason:** "universal" named a default nothing should have: a project says which packs it runs.
  The pack is never fingerprinted either, because the declaration is authoritative and dropping it
  is a deliberate choice rather than drift to detect.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Mechanism:** the id becomes `basics`, and activation is the project's
  `.claudinite-settings.json` declaration, seeded by bootstrap and backfilled into existing
  consumers by the nightly update.
- **Landed:** #232.

## 2026-07-11 · scope-changed · Package-driven skills: packs declare skills, mounts generated at session start (#234)
- **Reason:** a skill is content a pack contributes, like its prose and its checks, rather than a
  tree the engine owns.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Mechanism:** the manifest declares the pack's skills and the session-start mount is generated
  from that declaration.

The last pack on the shelf. Step 4 of #2169; the fourth and final backfill, after `claudinite`, `claudinite-canon-curation` and `claudinite-growth`.

Automerge policy: `packs/basics/provenance/`, `packs/basics/README.md`, `packs/basics/pack.mjs`. The manifest trim is part of the method.

## What landed

154 of 164 elements owed history (129 empty files, 25 holding only the references conversion's placeholder). The folder now carries **306 entries**, 267 of them written here, across 166 files with **none empty**:

| kind | n |
|---|---|
| born | 164 |
| reworded | 102 |
| moved | 13 |
| scope-changed | 9 |
| strengthened | 7 |
| trigger-changed | 4 |
| declined | 3 |
| converted | 3 |
| severity-changed | 1 |

History moved off the carriers and onto the entries it evidences:

| file | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `packs/basics/README.md` | 10066 | 9561 |
| `packs/basics/pack.mjs` | 2927 | 2510 |

The README's two tables were weighed and kept: they are a catalog of what the pack carries, not evidence. `pack.mjs`'s header lost the never-fingerprinted decision and the skills-moved-out sentence, both now `_pack` entries.

## 56 births corrected away from a compaction pass

The known defect of the brief, and by far the biggest correction here: it cannot follow a rule reworded on its way across a compaction, so it drafts a `born` at the compaction and does not flag it. The prior three packs cost 69, 13 and 13 corrections; this pack alone cost 56.

**#760** ("Rewrite RULES.md as situation-keyed rules") accounts for 43 of them on its own. Its body settles it: *"61 rules ... 4435 to 2985 words, with every rule preserved"*, and `packs/basics/RULES.md` at its parent is a 26.8 KB file carrying all of them. Each became a `reworded` at #760 with its `born` restored to the commit that actually decided it, the oldest being `5235b9d3` (2026-06-20). Two intermediate passes, #467 and #751, had to be gone behind twice for the same reason.

The rest: #1667 (3, now `moved`), #1711 (5), #1779 (2), #2016 (1), #2058 (2), and #28 (11, whose body names the eleven bullets it moved out of `engineeringPractices.md`). One pickaxe false trail: `barrier` drafted `born` at #242 because the word appears in an unrelated module; #267's body shows the check being created, so the birth moved there and the #242/#279/#283 drafts were dropped.

## `_pack.md`

Unlike `claudinite-growth`, whose `born` slot was already spent, this one was free: it holds the pack's creation as `universal` at #128, with eight later `scope-changed` entries for the shape changes (the rename and explicit declaration at #232, packs declaring skills, `requires`, skills moving inside packs, the barriers absorption, the improve-comments absorption from the retired tidy-repo).

## Known residue

- **15 files read "conversion only, history pending"** in `check`. For each, the placeholder's date *is* the birth, so the tool correctly kept it and that entry is the element's whole derived history. The residue is only that those borns are titled for the conversion rather than for their commit; the method forbids editing an existing entry, so they stand.
- **9 advisory `provenance-change-recorded` findings** at the Stop hook, on the files whose conversion placeholder was superseded. Sanctioned by the check's own fix text.
- **Four elements whose history the evidence does not reach** carry a `born` stating only the date, commit and mechanism, with no invented `Reason`.
- Nine superseded placeholders had their `Reason` and `Retire when` recovered by hand onto the entries they actually evidence, so nothing was dropped.
- The README cited the barriers absorption as #1681 and the tidy-repo retirement as #1839; the commits are #1684 and #1842, and the entries use those. The old numbers look like the tracking issues.

## Verification

- `provenance.mjs check basics`: exit 0, no fault, zero empty files
- `check_the_world.mjs`: exit 0, nothing naming `packs/basics`
- `check_the_work.mjs`: 0 blocking, 9 advisory (above)
- Diff scope: `packs/basics/provenance/`, `packs/basics/README.md`, `packs/basics/pack.mjs`, nothing else

Advances #2169.

entries.name: mcp__github__get_job_logs
entries.description:
Get logs for GitHub Actions workflow jobs.
Use this tool to retrieve logs for a specific job or all failed jobs in a workflow run.
For single job logs, provide job_id. For all failed jobs in a run, provide run_id with failed_only=true.

failed_only.description: When true, gets logs for all failed jobs in the workflow run specified by run_id. Requires run_id to be provided.

job_id.description: The unique identifier of the workflow job. Required when getting logs for a single job.

owner.description: Repository owner

return_content.description: Returns actual log content instead of URLs

run_id.description: The unique identifier of the workflow run. Required when failed_only is true to get logs for all failed jobs in the run.

tail_lines.description: Number of lines to return from the end of the log

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-tests

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
  (see-test-fail)
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
  (mechanism-meant-survive)
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
  (simulator-stateful-mechanism)
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
  (trusting-new-transform)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
  (test-stubs-exact)
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
  (test-dereferences-path)
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
  (test-value-set)
- **Naming the thing a fixture stands for** - invent the name (`acme-pack`, `acme-user`,
  `acme.example`) wherever the case holds for any name at all, and keep a real one only where that
  entity is what the case asserts about: a borrowed name reads as meaningful, collides with the
  real thing's own cases, and makes every later rename an edit of tests that were never about it.
  (fixture-names-invented)
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite. (testing-tasks-precondition)
- **Asserting on a record the code under test produced** — a finding, a parsed spec, a normalized declaration — assert the fields that code **computed**, and leave the ones it copied straight through from its own declaration or from your setup. A check selected by its id whose test then reads `finding.rule` back, or restates the `severity` its declaration set, is asserting the selector: it stays green however wrong the matching is, and goes red only when someone deliberately renames or re-grades the rule. One computed field identifies a record — the rest is your setup talking back to you.
  (asserting-record-code)
- **A coupling that must hold for every member of a set** — each task's id matching the directory it is discovered by, each check's `doc:` pointer resolving, each declaration validating — assert it once in a sweep that reads the whole set out of the tree, never in each member's own suite. The per-member copy only ever holds the members that happen to have a suite, so it under-covers and taxes at the same time: the shape is billed to each suite that has one while the members without one go unguarded.
  (coupling-must-hold)
- **Pinning the text a finding or error carries** — assert the part the code **derived** from the input (the version it tells you to bump to, the path it resolved, the term it names), and leave the static sentence alone. A remedy's wording is prose someone will improve, and asserted back it turns every rewording into a test edit while guarding nothing — those words were read straight out of the declaration the test already points at.
  (pinning-text-finding)
- **Sweeping a set** — a tree walk, a filter over a file's lines, a loop over discovered
  members — **pin how many members it covered**, beside the loop. An assertion reached only
  inside a loop, or only behind an `if`, says nothing about the members that never entered it,
  so a set that quietly shrinks — a renamed token, a moved directory, one call kind of two
  dropping out — leaves the survivors passing and reports that pass for the whole. A count read
  off the same source is the pin (`assert.ok(files.length >= 25)`), and a guard *inside* the
  loop needs its own, since the
  outer count says nothing about how many members reached the assertion behind it. (sweeping-set)
- **Reading the source *text* of a module the test could `import`** — asserting an identifier
  appears in it, or that one string precedes another in the file — inverts the signal: it goes
  red on a pure rename and stays green on a behaviour change that leaves the tokens in place.
  Grepping a *different* artifact is the two-artifact drift guard above and stays. Where the
  module is callable and a grep is still the only way in, report that its entry point does the
  whole job at once — that is worth more than the assertion. (reading-source-text)
- **Choosing the cases for a validator, parser or guard** — its own rejection branches are the
  list: for each, write the input that forces it. A branch nothing forces is either a promise
  no test holds or one the code can no longer reach, and both are worth finding. The gap
  clusters on the **present-but-unusable** input — the empty string, the directory that will
  not read, the module that throws on import — because absent and valid are the two cases
  everyone writes, while the field that is there and broken is the one that arrives in
  production. (choosing-cases-validator)
- **A comparison against a threshold, a deadline or an anchor instant** — test the value
  exactly **on** it, not only either side. `<=` and `<` differ on exactly one input, so a suite
  that samples comfortably around the boundary agrees with both and pins neither. Where a cron
  or a poll drives the comparison, that one input is the ordinary case rather than the edge: the
  run fires *at* the anchor. (comparison-against-threshold)
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
  (prefer-single-shared)
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
  (wire-format-encoding)
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism.
  (traceability-coverage-gate)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
  (golden-snapshot-test)
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
  (snapshot-golden-test-2)
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
  (round-trip-test)
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
  (new-e2e-heavy)
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
  (test-can-only)
- **A shared fixture helper is paid for by every test that calls it**, so build the part that is identical for every case — a scratch repo's `init` and seed commit, a migrated database, a compiled bundle — once per process and copy it, rather than rebuilding it per test.
  (shared-fixture-helper)

- **A test runner parallelises across FILES, so one file's serial runtime is a floor no worker count clears.** When a suite's CPU sits well below its core count, the idle cores are waiting on that file — give it intra-file concurrency, which more workers cannot substitute for.
  (test-runner-parallelises)

- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
  (run-suite-know)
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically.
  (test-code-drives)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
  (gate-fuzzy-quality)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
  (behavior-person-must)
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
  (snapshot-golden-test)
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
  (test-asserts-exact)
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
  (test-maintains-committed)
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
  (render-ui-image)
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
  (reproduce-reported-golden)
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).
  (image-golden-surface)
